groups.title: Questions 27–30
groups.instruction: Choose FOUR correct answers from the box A–G, next to questions 27–30.

transcript.text: You will hear a discussion between Fiona, who is the head of a college drama department
and a new tutor called Ed, who is preparing to run a voice coaching workshop for drama
students.
First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
Now, listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
Fiona: Right, Ed.
Well, I'm delighted that you've joined the drama department.
Now, part of my job is to support you during your probationary year.
So, let's ensure that you're clear about what you'll be doing in the first voice coaching
workshop you run next week.
Ed: OK.
Fiona: I'll be observing you working with the students as you show them how to project their voices
on stage.
I'll be evaluating how you cope with the practical activities as well as the theory.
And if all goes well, you'll then have finished the final stage of your voice coach diploma.
Ed: That'd be great, Fiona.
Anyway, I've thought through the workshop and I've done a plan to highlight the key areas
I intend to cover.
Fiona: Good.
Let's look at your plan.
Ed: OK.
Fiona: So, let's see.
I'm glad you've thought about seating patterns.
You say you want to begin with the student sitting in star-shaped patterns.
That's fine.
There are various seating patterns you can use at this stage.
I like trainees sitting cross-legged in a circle, other people like students in rows.
But actually, all these can be represented diagrammatically, which would be clearer
than going into lots of detailed explanations like you've done here.
Ed: Oh, OK.
But it doesn't matter which one I use at the beginning of a workshop.
Fiona: It's whatever you feel comfortable with.
Ed: Fine.
So, in the initial phase, I explain the objectives of the session.
Fiona: OK.
Then, in the first activity you say they should quickly rise, walk briskly around the room,
weaving in and out to avoid each other.
Ed: Yes.
I think it's important that they don't get in each other's way and that they learn to
move within a confined space, aware of other people, but primarily concentrating on their
own thoughts.
Fiona: Absolutely.
But in your plan, you've omitted to mention that in the second activity, you will get
the students to pair off.
So you need to rethink that section and include reasons why it's essential for them to listen
to each other talking.
It doesn't matter what they actually say.
And at the same time, get them to think about their posture because that governs their
lung capacity and most crucially, their breathing.
Ed: Right.
We'll do.
Fiona: OK.
Of course, a common issue in the UK is that we rehearse in small rooms, then transfer to
a larger stage.
So bearing in mind that voice projection is not shouting, later in the course, you'll
need to work in a much bigger space.
Ed: Does it have to be an enclosed space?
I suppose it does because ultimately they're going to work in a theatre.
Fiona: Ideally an enclosed space, but there's no reason why you couldn't go somewhere outdoors.
Although I'd avoid a very public space like a park.
Ed: Right.
Thanks.
Fiona: Well, your next activity on how to convey emotion on stage is fine, but your selection
of texts for the students to experience emotional depth leaves a little to be desired.
It's not enough to include a few extracts that you find enjoyable.
You need to consider the different kind of emotion that each extract should present
from sorrow through to ecstasy.
And classical stuff is all well and good, but include many more contemporary sources.
Ed: I understand.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27
to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
Fiona: Now out of the 20 books you list, some are more useful than others, and I think you
should flag up the disadvantages so that people don't waste money buying them.
Take vocal instruction.
I know I recommended it for you to read for its historical perspective, but bear in mind
it was written 30 years ago, and it shows, yeah, agreed.
Ed: I thought improve your accent was interesting, but it's very narrow in its outlook, don't
you think?
Fiona: Well, I'm not sure it's interesting.
And another one you need to warn people about is the actors handbook.
It's an expensive book, very useful, but according to the publishers, they're going to
reissue it with new colour photos, and at the moment it's out of print.
There aren't any second-hand copies out there, so tell them not to waste time looking for
it.
Ed: Oh, right.
I didn't know that.
Fiona: There's one more that I want to mention, and that's confident voice delivery.
It exaggerates its claims on how to be successful to such an extent that I think it is positively
misleading.
But, maybe unbiased.
Ed: Okay, I'll make a note of that, thanks.
Soot the other.
That is the end of part three.
You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part three.
